title: PAUL GRAHAM
subtitle: ESSAYS & NOTES
dek: 231 essays. 17 chapters. In his own words.
disclaimer: Personal reader. Not affiliated with Paul Graham or Y Combinator.

quotes.headline: Y Combinator. March 2005 (This essay is derived from a talk at the Harvard Computer Society.) You need three things to create a successful startup: to start with good people, to make something customers actually want, and to spend as little money as possible.
Y Combinator. March 2007 (This essay is derived from talks at the 2007 Startup School and the Berkeley CSUA.) We've now been doing Y Combinator long enough to have some data about success rates.
quotes.source: Why to Not Not Start a Startup

quotes.headline: Y Combinator. October 2014 (This essay is derived from a guest lecture in Sam Altman's startup class at Stanford.
Y Combinator's 7th birthday was March 11. As usual we were so busy we didn't notice till a few days after.
Y Combinator. October 2008 The economic situation is apparently so grim that some experts fear we may be in for a stretch as bad as the mid seventies.
quotes.source: Why to Start a Startup in a Bad Economy

quotes.headline: There are now exactly 800 YC alumni, including the batch that's just starting.
Starting a startup is one of the few tasks where inexperience is no barrier. Because if you do it right you get the experience en route.
Skip the preamble. If you have something interesting to say, just start right in on it.

In some kinds of work, doing something faster than your peers is a sign of ability. But starting a startup at 16 doesn't mean you're 50% better at startups than Larry Page. It's more like stumbling into a room.
Don't start a startup where you need to go through someone else to get users.

Since I was about 9 I've been puzzled by the apparent contradiction between being made of matter that behaves in a predictable way, and the feeling that I could choose to do whatever I wanted. At the time I had a self-interested motive for exploring the question.
Y Combinator. April 2010 The best way to come up with startup ideas is to ask yourself the question: what do you wish someone would make for you?
Y Combinator. November 2012 The way to get startup ideas is not to try to think of startup ideas.
(Someone fed my essays into GPT to make something that could answer questions based on them, then asked it where good ideas come from. The answer was ok, but not what I would have said.

Startups in 137 chars: Make something someone specific needs, launch
fast, let users show you what to change, change it, repeat last two.
A founder on @RonConway: "Ron + SV have been fantastic. I really understand now why people want them in their corner."
At first the question is "What would be cool to build?" Then it's "What do people want?" Then it's "What gets you growth?"
Make something people want. #GoodAdviceIn4Words Finally a masstag I can participate in.
It's dangerous for an organization to become so established that normal people want to work there.
5 yo's first startup idea: pyjamas lined with fluff. I've heard worse.
Y Combinator. July 2013 One of the most common types of advice we give at Y Combinator is to do things that don't scale.
High-fiber diet : peasant's diet :: doing things that don't scale : how Henry Ford got started.
The best protection against competitor x is to do things that are contrary to their DNA.

When we do things that work, we rarely understand exactly why. We do them unconsciously, or because of tradition, or because we stumbled onto them. A lot of the value of essay writing is in figuring out why things that work do work.
Y Combinator. September 2012 A startup is a company designed to grow fast.

When I talk to a startup that's been operating for more than 8 or 9 months, the first thing I want to know is almost always the same. Assuming their expenses remain constant and their revenue growth is what it has been over the last several months, do they make it to…
A startup just sent me a status report beginning "last week we had the worst growth week since launch."  They will succeed.
Spectral signature of a doomed startup: "We're rewriting everything, and we'll go back to focusing on growth afterward."
Startups that graph their growth rate (e.g. Coinbase, Zenefits) do well.  Only the toughest can face graphs where flat is good.
Twitter is really pushing engagement features lately.  Is this a sign organic growth is slowing?
The best way to increase a startup's growth rate is to make the product so good people recommend it to their friends.
Suggestion for really tough founders: instead of graphing revenue, graph growth rate thereof. Now you're fighting for flat.

Another startup fortune cookie:

"Your growth is slow because your product is not appealing enough."
What's the trick to fundraising? Rapid growth. What's the trick for getting growth? A great product.
Y Combinator. August 2008 Raising money is the second hardest part of starting a startup.
Y Combinator. November 2005 Venture funding works like gears.
Y Combinator. September 2010 The reason startups have been using more convertible notes in angel rounds is that they make deals close faster.

Y Combinator. August 2010 Two years ago I wrote about what I called "a huge, unexploited opportunity in startup funding:" the growing disconnect between VCs, whose current business model requires them to invest large amounts, and a large class of startups that need less than…
Convertible notes have won.  Every investment so far in this YC batch (and there have been a lot) has been done on a convertible note.
Walking 3 blocks on University Ave, I ran into 5 separate YC-funded startups.  (YC is not based in Palo Alto.)
The most common comparison this YC cycle: "We're the Mint.com of blank."
We got so many good applications for the winter 2011 YC cycle that we're going to do 6 days of interviews instead of 4.
Working on talk for #ycnyc tonight. Startup hubs as antidote.
YC is now getting just over 1 application per minute.
Y Combinator. January 2012 There are great startup ideas lying around unexploited right under our noses.

(This essay is derived from a talk at the 2006 Startup School.) The startups we've funded so far are pretty quick, but they seem quicker to learn some lessons than others. I think it's because some things about startups are kind of counterintuitive.
quotes.source: The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn

quotes.headline: Y Combinator. October 2006 In the Q & A period after a recent talk, someone asked what made startups fail.
Y Combinator. Watch how this essay was written.
"Working is so boring that I don't want to do it even when I'm supposed to when I grow up." – 4 y.o. watching me read YC applications
Big discoveries often consist of showing that something that seemed boring is more interesting than others realized.
The trouble with making boring tasks amusing for small kids is that they then want to do them over and over.
All other things being equal, assume the more boring explanation is true.
Yoga gives you back the 3 things you lose as you age: strength, flexibility, and balance. That's why it seems so boring to kids.
It would be in the interest of good IoT cos to create a free security layer. Otherwise consumers may avoid the whole category.
Y Combinator. October 2010 (I wrote this for Forbes, who asked me to write something about the qualities we look for in founders.
quotes.source: What We Look for in Founders

quotes.headline: At a YC event last week Brian Chesky gave a talk that everyone who was there will remember. Most founders I talked to afterward said it was the best they'd ever heard.
Y Combinator. December 2010 Someone we funded is talking to VCs now, and asked me how common it was for a startup's founders to retain control of the board after a series A round.
Inc recently asked me who I thought were the 5 most interesting startup founders of the last 30 years. How do you decide who's the most interesting?
Y Combinator. March 2009 A couple days ago I finally got being a good startup founder down to two words: relentlessly resourceful.
Nearly all the most successful founders are revolutionaries.  They want power, not money.  That makes them hard to stop.
"I tried to be as cynical as I could but it still wasn't cynical enough." -- a w2013 founder on investors
Everyone's practicing for Demo Day, and Doordash just delivered us Indian food for 30 people!  The founders are so happy.
Every time I have any interaction with Watsi or its founders, I come away feeling better.
Exercise for founders: How would you describe your idea without using the word "platform?"

"...the mere consciousness of an engagement will sometimes worry a whole day." � Charles Dickens July 2009 One reason programmers dislike meetings so much is that they're on a different type of schedule from other people. Meetings cost them more.
If you collected lists of techniques for doing great work in a lot of different fields, what would the intersection look like? I decided to find out by making it.
Y Combinator. January 2006 To do something well you have to like it.
quotes.source: How to Do What You Love

quotes.headline: There's some debate about whether it's a good idea to "follow your passion." In fact the question is impossible to answer with a simple yes or no. Sometimes you should and sometimes you shouldn't, but the border between should and shouldn't is very complicated.
quotes.source: When To Do What You Love

quotes.headline: Congrats to @foundersatwork on 10 years of Startup School.
Work on making users love you, not investors. (And then investors will.)
Microsoft could probably hurt Google more by shutting down Bing (and exposing Google to antitrust action) than by continuing to work on it.
I measure an idea for something to work on by how many of me there would have to be before I'd have one work on it.
One thing young people don't pay enough attention to when deciding what to work on is how you win in each type of job.

Projects that yield great results often wouldn't seem promising to a rational person. Fortunately some people have a compensating irrationality: they're so interested in the project that they'll work on it for its own sake.
It would be convenient if you could do great work by working only moderately hard. Maybe there are some people who can. But I can't think of any.

"...Copernicus' aesthetic objections to [equants] provided one essential motive for his rejection of the Ptolemaic system...." - Thomas Kuhn, The Copernican Revolution "All of us had been trained by Kelly Johnson and believed fanatically in his insistence that an airplane…
(This essay is derived from a talk at the Cambridge Union.) When I was a kid, I'd have said there wasn't. My father told me so.
quotes.source: Is There Such a Thing as Good Taste?

quotes.headline: When I was in high school I spent a lot of time imitating bad writers. What we studied in English classes was mostly fiction, so I assumed that was the highest form of writing.
The Twitter redesign will be the best thing that ever happened to Twitter clients. A secret plan to cut server loads?
The GMail redesign illustrates the distinction between high production values and good design.
We installed Nest thermostats at YC and frankly it has been a disaster.  Design does not end with the case, guys.
I take back that tweet about the Nest thermostats.  Their design doesn't end with the case.  I just didn't understand them.
GMail's bad redesigns keep pushing me closer to funding a new email co just so I can use it.
The latest Twitter redesign is going to make it easy for me to achieve my goal of using the Internet less.
The new building Kate Courteau designed for Y Combinator is a masterpiece.
Remember the essays you had to write in high school? Topic sentence, introductory paragraph, supporting paragraphs, conclusion.
Despite its title this isn't meant to be the best essay. My goal here is to figure out what the best essay would be like.
Here's a simple trick for getting more people to read what you write: write in spoken language. Something comes over most people when they start writing.
I try to write using ordinary words and simple sentences. That kind of writing is easier to read, and the easier something is to read, the more deeply readers will engage with it.

I'm usually reluctant to make predictions about technology, but I feel fairly confident about this one: in a couple decades there won't be many people who can write. One of the strangest things you learn if you're a writer is how many people have trouble writing.
What should an essay be? Many people would say persuasive.
The software battle between Obama and Romney is probably important enough that someone should write a book about it.
If anyone is wondering, I'm trying to write a complete guide to fundraising in time for Demo Day (Aug 20).
30 Rock is what would happen if the writers took over a TV show.
When the press writes about a topic you know well, you realize every news article you've read could have been equally mistaken.

Y Combinator. March 2012 One of the more surprising things I've noticed while working on Y Combinator is how frightening the most ambitious startup ideas are.
Just under 14% of Y Combinator applications so far are no-idea applications.
New store on University Ave! What will it be? Folded banner inside says "From idea to IPO." In the back, an orange wall. Ack.
Now that people pitch me nonprofits too, I sometimes have to ask which type the idea is.  Probably not a good sign.
"I feel like ginormous philtrums could be a whole art style." – Trevor Blackwell's brilliant idea for the day

"The idea that some lives matter less is the root of all that is wrong with the world."

– Paul Farmer
I wish there were a less pretentious alternative to "bricoleur." It's an important idea but I can't bring myself to use that word.
"The way to tell a great idea is that, when people hear it, they say, 'Gee, I could have thought of that.'" – Feynman, quoted by Townes
I finally realized today why politics and religion yield such uniquely useless discussions. As a rule, any mention of religion on an online forum degenerates into a religious argument.
Have you ever seen an old photo of yourself and been embarrassed at the way you looked? Did we actually dress like that?
It struck me recently how few of the most successful people I know are mean. There are exceptions, but remarkably few.
Oddly enough it didn't occur to me that predicting failure for mean people would evoke a lot of mean responses...
If you're the best, your competitors will lie about you and/or themselves. They have no choice. They can't say "we're inferior, but choose us anyway."

"Burgeoning" is one of those words that doesn't occur in spoken English. You only see it when people switch into their fancy writing diction. 

It's getting real big, they think. But I can't say that. I know, I'll say that it's burgeoning.

You can measure the level of intolerance in a society by whether you can say that there are things that are true, but that you can't say. Every society I know of has had them. When the fact that yours has them becomes one of them, you've reached level 2.

I experience the feeling of deja vu more often while using Twitter than while doing anything else. It's weirdly self-similar. I suspect this is a warning sign of its futility, though I can't say for sure.
One way you can tell real experts is that they hedge less. They'll tell you what's *not* the case. People with merely moderate expertise can't say that, because they're not sure.
Y Combinator. May 2004 (This essay was originally published in Hackers & Painters.) If you wanted to get rich, how would you do it?
How do you convert between wealth and income tax? If a government imposes a wealth tax of 1%, what's the equivalent in income tax?
quotes.source: How to Convert Between Wealth and Income Tax

quotes.headline: Larry & Sergey didn't get rich by a "transfer of wealth from the middle class and the poor."

Me: If a friend asked how to get rich, what would you tell them?

6 yo: Do something nobody else has done. Don't copy ideas. And make something lots of people actually want.

"If you want to get rich, don't do it for the money."

– Caleb Williams

The amount of equity you'll get in a startup decreases exponentially as your employee number increases. If you want to get rich from a startup, you have to be there early, either as a founder or an early employee.
The idea that you can get rich without doing a lot of work is so false that you can use its falsity as a heuristic. You can make more by deliberately chasing hard problems.

To get rich, do work where you get paid in proportion to the number of customers you satisfy instead of the number of hours you work. Not all work of this kind will make you rich, but nearly all work that can make you rich is of this kind.
Being bitter about wealth is a good way to ensure you'll never become rich. Why would you do anything to bring you closer to something you despise?
Great cities attract ambitious people. You can sense it when you walk around one.
Y Combinator. October 2011 If you look at a list of US cities sorted by population, the number of successful startups per capita varies by orders of magnitude.
(This essay is derived from a keynote at Xtech.) Startups happen in clusters. There are a lot of them in Silicon Valley and Boston, and few in Chicago or Miami.
After the last talk I gave, one of the organizers got up on the stage to deliver an impromptu rebuttal. That never happened before.
quotes.source: Why to Move to a Startup Hub

Old people have learned to avoid many mistakes the young make, but they still make mistakes constantly.  The supply is infinite.
Doing things that impress your peers is a good heuristic when you're old but a bad one when you're young.
The commonest negotiation between our kids is what animal the younger shall be.
Politicians don't yet get that attacking new economic forms makes them seem out of touch to the young, just as with music.
One difference between LA and SF: the number of old men with much younger girlfriends.

People love Lisp for much the same reason they love Lego.
Nerd triumph of the day: apparent mach diamonds in men's room yield plausible estimate of fluorescent light flicker rate.
The nerdy earnestness of people's interest in cryptocurrency is to me the most promising sign about it. Like microcomputers in the 1970s.

Hello, I'm a Lisp hacker. You may know me from my greatest hits, including "The parentheses are not an issue," "It's not intrinsically for AI," and "You just used a forum written in Lisp to post that comment saying nothing is written in Lisp."
Any optimistic project creates the opportunity to seem clever by cynically dismissing it. Fortunately (or unfortunately) most nerds learn this at about 12. By adulthood it has little effect on them.
Lisp's parentheses are the bumps on the top of Lego.

Needed some code from On Lisp yesterday and happened to read a chunk of it. If you've ever wondered whether, after someone writes a book, the stuff in the book is in their head ever after, the answer is definitely no.
